title: On-call & Incident Response Playbook
author: Priya Shah
content:
Summary
-------
This playbook documents Redwood Inference's on-call and incident response process: detection, triage, escalation, runbooks, postmortem expectations, on-call rotations, game day exercises, and customer-facing status/update templates. It is intended for SREs, platform engineers, support, and engineering leads who may be involved during incidents.

Scope
-----
- Applies to all production services that support hosted API, Dedicated, and Private deployments.
- Covers Sev0-Sev3 incidents (definitions below), escalation flows, runbook usage, and postmortem cadence.
- Does not replace service-specific runbooks; it defines standards and templates to follow.

1) Incident severity & when to use them
------------------------------------
- Sev0 (Platform down / Data loss): Total platform outage affecting all customers or confirmed data loss. Requires immediate page and executive alerts. Target response: 5 minutes.
- Sev1 (Major degradation): Core API unavailable or >50% customers impacted; or p99 latency or error rate exceeds SLOs by a large margin for >5 minutes. Target response: 15 minutes.
- Sev2 (Partial degradation): Significant feature-level impacts (e.g., embeddings failing for a region), elevated error rates affecting subset customers. Target response: 30 minutes.
- Sev3 (Minor / non-urgent): Degraded telemetry, single-customer issues without broader impact, or scheduled maintenance questions. Target response: next business day.

Severity triggers (examples)
- API error rate (5m) > 5% -> Sev1 if sustained + customer impact.
- p95 latency > 500ms for >10 minutes -> Sev2; if p95 > 1500ms or p99 high -> Sev1.
- Availability < 99.5% across region for 10 minutes -> Sev1/Sev0 depending on scope.

2) Detection & initial triage checklist
-------------------------------------
1. Acknowledge alert immediately in PagerDuty and Slack #oncall.
2. Create an incident in the incident tracker (use our incident template). Include: title, severity, impacted services/regions, start time, initial symptoms, on-call owner.
3. Run quick health checks (examples):
   - Kubernetes: kubectl -n <ns> get pods -o wide | egrep "CrashLoopBackOff|ImagePullBackOff"
   - Load balancers: check cloud console (GCP/AWS) for unhealthy targets
   - DB/Cache: SELECT 1 against primary; check replica lag (pg_stat_replication) or redis INFO replication
   - Queues: check backlog in SQS/Kafka consumer lag
4. Post initial findings in Slack incident thread and update incident ticket.

3) Roles & responsibilities
---------------------------
- Incident Commander (IC): owns coordination, communications, and timeline. Responsibilities: set severity, assign roles, ensure updates.
- Tech Lead / Service Owner: leads technical investigation, executes runbooks, coordinates with IC.
- Communications Lead: drafts customer-facing messages and status page updates.
- Scribe / Timeline owner: notes timeline events, commands run, decisions, and mitigation steps.
- Secondary on-call: backup to IC for escalation and follow-ups.

Escalation policy (high-level)
- If primary on-call cannot acknowledge in 5 minutes (Sev0) / 15 minutes (Sev1), PagerDuty automatically escalates to secondary and then to on-call manager.
- For Sev0, notify CTO and Head of SRE immediately once incident ticket is created.

4) Runbook usage & template
---------------------------
- Every production service must have a one-click runbook accessible from the incident ticket. The runbook should include: symptoms, quick checks, common mitigations, rollback commands, safety checks, and contact list.
- Runbook template (copy into service repo):

  Title: <service-name> emergency runbook
  Last updated: YYYY-MM-DD
  Owners: @team, pagerduty-policy

  Quick checks:
  - check service health endpoint: curl -sSf https://<service>/health || true
  - list pods: kubectl -n <ns> get pods -l app=<service>
  - check logs (last 5m): kubectl -n <ns> logs -l app=<service> --since=5m | tail -n 100
  - check queue/backlog metrics: (link to dashboard)

  Known mitigations:
  1) Restart failing pods: kubectl -n <ns> rollout restart deployment/<deploy> (only when safe)
  2) Scale up replicas: kubectl -n <ns> scale deploy/<deploy> --replicas=<n>
  3) Toggle feature flag / disable non-critical workers (link to FF service)
  4) Failover DB read traffic to replica (if documented and approved)

  Rollback checklist:
  - Identify last deploy: kubectl -n <ns> rollout history deploy/<deploy>
  - Rollback to previous: kubectl -n <ns> rollout undo deploy/<deploy> --to-revision=<rev>
  - Validate health endpoints and metrics for 10 minutes post-rollback

  Safety & communications:
  - If mitigation could cause data loss or customer-visible change, get IC sign-off.

5) Communication cadence & templates
----------------------------------
- Internal updates: every 15m for Sev0/Sev1 until containment. Post in Slack #incidents and update incident ticket.
- Customer/status page cadence: initial acknowledgement within 30 minutes for Sev0/Sev1, updates every 60 minutes until resolution, then final resolution message within 2 hours of full recovery.

Customer-facing templates (copy/paste)
- Initial acknowledgement (30m):
  Subject: Incident: <short-summary> \u2014 We're investigating
  Body: We are aware of an issue affecting <services/regions>. Our engineering team is investigating. Impact: <brief impact>. Next update: in 60 minutes or sooner. Reference: https://status.redwood.example.com/incidents/<id>

- Update (periodic):
  Subject: Update: <short-summary> \u2014 <time since start>
  Body: Current status: <what changed>. Actions taken: <steps>. Next update: in 60 minutes or when there is material change.

- Resolution:
  Subject: Incident resolved: <short-summary>
  Body: Impact: <summary of customers/signals>. Root cause (preliminary): <short>. Mitigation: <steps taken>. Full postmortem: <link when available>.

Status page guidance
- Use the status page to post the short acknowledgement and to publish updates. Keep the status page concise and technical enough for customers to understand scope and expected ETA. 

6) Postmortem process & template
--------------------------------
- Postmortem required for Sev0/Sev1 incidents and at manager discretion for Sev2. Draft within 72 hours; final postmortem published within 10 business days. Postmortems are public-internal by default.

- Postmortem template (required fields):
  - title (one-line)
  - severity and duration (start/end times in UTC)
  - summary (two-sentence impact)
  - root cause (summary)
  - detection (how and when it was detected)
  - timeline (minute-resolution for first 2 hours, then aggregated)
  - mitigation & remediation steps (what fixed it and permanent fixes planned)
  - customer impact (who was affected, outage windows)
  - monitoring & alerting gaps
  - action items (owner, due date, verification plan)
  - lessons learned

Example action item format:
- Migrate health-check logic from service to an independent monitor \u2014 owner: @devops-team, due: 2026-03-15, verification: game day scheduled Q2.

7) On-call rotations & handoffs
-------------------------------
- Rotation model: primary and secondary weekly rotations for eng-sre. Each rotation is 7 days, starting Monday 00:00 UTC.
- Handoff checklist (to be posted to Slack during changeover):
  1) Primary posts weekly handoff message in #oncall with: active incidents, open action items, and on-call notes.
  2) Check scheduled maintenance for conflicts.
  3) Verify PagerDuty escalation policies and contact details.
  4) Confirm access to runbooks and service dashboards.
- Vacation & escalation: If primary cannot cover, update PagerDuty to delegate the shift and notify the team.

8) Game days & run-throughs
--------------------------
- Cadence: quarterly game days led by SRE manager. One cross-functional game day per quarter with product and platform engineers.
- Goals: validate runbooks, test failover, rehearse communications, and surface automation/network gaps.
- Typical scenarios: control-plane outage, region-level network partition, database primary failover, and high error-rate cascading failures.
- Post-game-day: publish a short report with findings and action items assigned in the incident tracker.

9) Monitoring, alerting & SLOs (example thresholds)
--------------------------------------------------
- Service availability SLO: 99.95% monthly for Redwood API. Error budget management process lives in SLO playbook.
- Example alerts:
  - API 5m error rate > 5% -> paging alert (Sev1 candidate)
  - p95 latency > 1500ms for 5m -> paging alert (Sev1 if customer impact)
  - CPU > 90% cluster-wide for 10m -> warn (Sev2)
  - Disk < 10% free on primary -> paging (Sev1/Sev0 depending on service criticality)

10) Incident tooling & artifacts
--------------------------------
- Incident tracker: create an incident using /incidents/new (internal tool). Include severity, links to runbooks, dashboards, and status page ID.
- PagerDuty: ensure policies match runbooks and team ownership.
- Slack: use #incidents for internal updates; create a dedicated incident channel (e.g., #incident-1234) for threaded discussion.
- Postmortems live in Confluence under /oncall-and-incident-response/postmortems with cross-links to the incident tracker and status page.

11) Verification & follow-up
---------------------------
- After mitigation, monitor customer-facing metrics for at least 60 minutes for Sev1 and 30 minutes for Sev2 before declaring resolution.
- Action items must have owners and due dates. SRE manager will verify completion and assign a verification step (test or game-day) before closing the action.

12) Appendix: common CLI snippets & dashboards
----------------------------------------------
- Kubernetes quick health: kubectl -n prod get pods -l app=<svc> -o wide
- Check last deploy: kubectl -n prod rollout history deployment/<deploy>
- Redis info and replication: redis-cli INFO replication
- Postgres replica lag: SELECT application_name, pg_catalog.pg_xlog_location_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), replay_lsn) AS bytes_behind FROM pg_stat_replication;
- Dashboards: link to API latency dashboard, error-rate dashboard, cluster health (list links in service-runbooks).

13) Frequently asked questions
-----------------------------
Q: When do we declare an incident over?
A: After root cause mitigations are in place, customer impact has returned to baseline, and metrics are stable for the verification window. IC must post a resolution message with timeframe and planned follow-ups.

Q: Who approves customer communications?
A: Communications lead under the IC signs off on customer-facing messaging; for enterprise customers with dedicated CSMs, loop in Customer Success for tailored comms.
